title: Who Passed? Filter, Sort and Pick
oneLiner: Pair up names with scores, keep those at or above the pass mark, sort best first with ties alphabetical, and return just the names.
keyTakeaway: Many queries are a pipeline: pair up (Zip / zip), filter (Where / if), sort (OrderByDescending.ThenBy / a tuple key with a negated number), then project (Select / the expression of a comprehension). Write it as one chain and read it top to bottom.
explanation:
Write PassingNames(names, scores, passMark). names[i] scored scores[i]; return the names of everyone whose score is at least passMark, highest score first, and alphabetical among equal scores. For names ["ann", "bob", "cy", "dee"], scores [70, 45, 90, 70] and a pass mark of 50, the answer is ["cy", "ann", "dee"]: cy has 90, then ann and dee tie on 70. Nobody passing gives an empty list. Names are lowercase letters.

In C#: names.Zip(scores) pairs them up, giving tuples with First and Second; then Where, OrderByDescending on the score, ThenBy on the name (with StringComparer.Ordinal to compare by character code), and Select the name.

In Python: zip(names, scores) pairs them; a comprehension keeps the passing pairs; sorted with key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]) puts high scores first (negating a number reverses its order) and breaks ties by name; a last comprehension picks the names. This is the filter, sort and project pipeline from the LINQ and Comprehensions lesson.

complexity.note: Pairing and filtering are O(n); sorting the passing pairs is O(n log n) and dominates. The pairs and the result take O(n) space.

referenceSolutions.python:
def passing_names(names, scores, pass_mark):
    passed = [(name, score) for name, score in zip(names, scores) if score >= pass_mark]
    passed.sort(key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0]))   # high score first, then name
    return [name for name, _ in passed]
